ruling.reasoning:
The trip was RydeTAXI, metered [F8], so extra kilometres enter the fare and RD-2's metered branch governs: the refund is Σ(extra_km of non-exempt segments) × this trip's per-km rate [RD-2]. The rate is the fare record's distance fare ÷ distance km: $29.44 ÷ 20.88 km = $1.4100/km [F5][F8][RD-2]. There is exactly one off-route segment, F4 (14:33–14:48, 7.45 km driven where the optimal route covers 2.40 km, +5.05 km, up to 1987 m off the corridor) [F4][RD-1].

RD-5 consent: before the segment began at 14:33 the rider wrote at 14:30 "Just take whichever way is faster lah, I'm late." [F10][F4]. Read in context, that is a general route choice, so the segment's finding is "counts" on the ground driver_errand: the driver's own post-trip statement admits "I went round the jam and stopped briefly to collect something on the way" [F12], and the system record places a 4 min 0 s standstill at 14:38–14:42, inside the off-route window and at neither endpoint (7443 m from pickup, 6033 m from drop-off) [F2][F4]. claims.assertion: The trip was driven 20.9 km against an optimal 15.6 km (+5.3 km, +34%) and took 38.5 min against 21.7 min estimated, so on its face the meter ran well above the quoted trip (F1, F3); the excess is billed at $1.4100/km (F5).

There is exactly one off-route segment on the record: 14:33–14:48, 7.45 km driven where the optimal route covers 2.40 km, adding 5.05 km and reaching 1987 m from the optimal route (F4); no other gps-detour fact exists, so RD-2 can be computed on this single segment.

The rider's only message before the segment was Chat #2 at 14:30: “Just take whichever way is faster lah, I'm late.” (F10), which is a general route choice and under RD-5 covers only the route taken to reach the destination — it does not cover a four-minute stop for the driver's own purpose.

The driver's own written statement admits an errand: “I went round the jam and stopped briefly to collect something on the way.” (F12); that stop is a purpose of the driver's own that no rider message asked for, so the segment of the loop that exists to serve it is a driver errand and cannot be excused by the rider's general route authorisation (F10).

The record matches that admission: the car stood still for 4 min 0 s at 14:38–14:42 at a point 7443 m from pickup and 6033 m from drop-off, i.e. not a pickup or drop-off point and inside the off-route window (F2, F4).

The rider's message was sent at 14:30, before the segment started at 14:33 (F10, F4), so the timing requirement in RD-5 is met only as to the general choice of route; it reaches no further, because the rider named no road and no stop.

The driver's congestion excuse is only partly supported by the accepted evidence: the only speed-band record touching the optimal corridor is CENTRAL EXPRESSWAY band 2 (10–19 km/h) during 14:11–14:33 (F13), and no traffic incident at all was recorded near the route in the trip window (F16); nothing in the traffic record explains a detour up to 1987 m off the corridor after 14:33 or the 4-minute stop (F2, F4).
Under RD-2 the refundable mileage on the unexcused segment is the extra distance actually billed: $7.46 (5.29 km × $1.4100/km) as itemised in the fare record (F5).

The $1.15 waiting fee was billed as 4.4 min × $0.26/min (F6) and corresponds to the 4-minute mid-trip stop that served no rider request (F2, F12); the only published mid-trip charge Ryde allows on an agreed change of destination is $3.00 and this was not an agreed change of destination, so a mid-trip stop for the driver's own purpose has no billable basis (F10, F12).
The driver has 4 disputes and 2 upheld in the last 90 days over 571 trips (F19); this supports an account-review flag but does not itself decide the route finding.

weaknesses: The rider did authorise a route choice: Chat #2 at 14:30 says “Just take whichever way is faster lah” (F10) and it precedes the 14:33 segment start (F4), so the driver will argue the whole 5.05 km loop is general_route_consent under RD-5 — my answer is that the loop left the corridor by up to 1987 m and contained a stop for the driver's own purpose (F2, F12), which a general authorisation does not cover.

The driver will partly succeed on RD-4: CENTRAL EXPRESSWAY was recorded at band 2 (10–19 km/h) during 14:11–14:33 (F13), so some deviation early in the segment may be excused as congestion, which would shrink the unexcused kilometres below the 5.05 km I claim; note also that a lone band-2 record is only corroborative under RD-4(b) and no incident was recorded (F16).

The chat record is short (two messages) and the driver's statement (F12) is the only direct evidence that the stop was his own errand; the 4-minute stationary period (F2) and its location off both endpoints are consistent with it, but the purpose of the stop rests on his own words — though it is an admission against his interest, not a contested claim.

The traffic-corridor match is the driver's strongest factual point and the record does not name a road for the driven segment; if the judge reads the loop as an ordinary congestion-avoidance route rather than an errand, the segment falls to general_route_consent and only the $1.15 stop-related item survives.

claims.assertion: The rider gave a general route delegation before the deviation began: at 14:30 she wrote "Just take whichever way is faster lah, I'm late." (F10), which follows the driver's 14:29 message that the Central Expressway was jamming ahead (F9); the off-route segment started at 14:33, after that message (F4), so the segment is covered by general route consent under RD-5.

The reroute was not a blind detour: the Central Expressway was recorded at speed band 2 (10–19 km/h) during 14:11–14:33 (F13), the road the driver told the rider was building up (F9), so the driver chose a faster corridor to honour the rider's "whichever way is faster" instruction (F10).

The only recorded stop is 4 min 0 s at (1.3032, 103.8613), 14:38–14:42, 7443 m from pickup and 6033 m from drop-off (F2); the rider agreed to a route, not to a stop, so that stop is a stop of the driver's own and is not covered by the route consent (F9, F10), while the rider's message asked for a faster way to her destination, not for a collection errand (F10).

The complaint about the meter is quantifiable: the excess distance billed is $7.46 (5.29 km × $1.4100/km, this trip's distance fare ÷ distance km) (F5), and the in-trip waiting fee billed is $1.15 (4.4 min × $0.26/min) (F6), both computed from the fare breakdown (F8); the base, distance, time and platform components are ordinary metered components.

The device record does not tie the 5.05 km extra segment (F4) to any road named by the rider, and no traffic incident is recorded near the route during the trip window (F16), while the built-up corridor was the Central Expressway itself (F13).

The chat record is complete and fully timestamped, 2 messages, with the rider's consent message sent at 14:30 before the 14:33 segment start (F11, F10, F4), so there is no G12 incompleteness barring a ruling on the route segment.

weaknesses: The rider's own complaint says "I said take any faster way, not stop somewhere for four minutes", and the GPS fact F2 (4 min 0 s stationary at a point 7443 m from pickup, 6033 m from drop-off) plus F12 (driver statement "stopped briefly to collect something on the way") put the stop squarely on my side of the line: under RD-3(b) and RD-5 a general route consent does not cover the driver's own errand, so the 4.4 min waiting billed at $1.15 (F6) is the rider's strongest point.

The magnitude of the deviation undercuts my "faster way" argument: 5.05 km added over 7.45 km driven where the optimal route covers 2.40 km, up to 1987 m off the optimal route (F4), and actual 20.9 km vs optimal 15.6 km, +34% (F1), which the rider will say no faster route requires.

The rider's message names no route at all (F10), so my consent is only general; under RD-5 general consent still does not cover a loop that reaches nothing (the stop at F2) or the driver's own purpose, and I cannot tie the driven segment to any named road because no fact names one (F4, F10).

The rider's profile is clean: 4.1 years, rating 4.8, 0 disputes in 90 days (F18), while my own profile shows 4 disputes and 2 upheld in 90 days (F19), which the rider will use to argue pattern rather than one-off, and which keeps RD-6 alive if any part of the deviation is upheld.

points.response: Concede that the message at 14:30 (F10) precedes the 14:33 segment start (F4) and is a general route authorisation under RD-5, but a general authorisation covers only the route to the destination and not the driver's own errand, which he admits in F12 — so it cannot excuse the whole 5.05 km segment.

F13 shows band 2 only during 14:11–14:33 on the Central Expressway, while the segment ran to 14:48 and reached 1987 m off the optimal route (F4), and no traffic incident was recorded anywhere near the route (F16) — a single earlier band-2 reading does not, under RD-4(b), justify what happened after 14:33.

The driver himself puts the stop outside the consent he relies on (F2, F12) — 4 min 0 s at 14:38–14:42 at a point 7443 m from pickup and 6033 m from drop-off (F2) — and that is exactly the rider's point, so the $1.15 stop-related waiting fee (F6) cannot stand.

The fare items are agreed as figures (F5, F6, F8), but RD-2 requires the unexcused kilometres to be refunded, and the driver's own admission of a personal errand (F12) removes the excuse for the segment in which the stop lies (F2, F4), so $7.46 is refundable and not just $1.15.

Correct that no fact ties the segment to a named road (F4, F10) — which is why I do not claim named_road_tied; my ground is the driver's admitted errand, which is not a route claim at all and needs no road name (F12).
Agreed: the record is timestamped and complete (F11), so there is no G12 bar and the judge can rule on the segment on the record as it stands.

My own claim C3 stands only as narrowed by D1: the 14:30 message is a general route authorisation reaching the route to the destination, and reaches neither the personal errand admitted in F12 nor the 4 min 0 s standstill at F2.

Unchanged and now unchallenged on its core: the driver's written statement F12 admits collecting something en route, the record places a 4 min 0 s stop inside the off-route window at a non-endpoint location (F2, F4), and RD-5 does not extend a general route authorisation to the driver's own business.

Conceded as to arithmetic only: F1 and F3 record actual 20.9 km vs optimal 15.6 km and 38.5 min vs 21.7 min estimated. But RD-1 liability turns on whether each segment is exempt, and the single gps-detour segment ran 14:33–14:48 (F4) only 3 minutes after the rider's own instruction at 14:30 to take whichever way was faster (F10); the pre-consent deviation is therefore explained, not unexplained.

Accepted that F4 is the only off-route segment, but a single segment is reviewed as a whole under RD-3/RD-4/RD-5, and my reading of the record is that the segment is covered by the rider's general route delegation (F10) because it began after her 14:30 message (F4), with the stop inside it dealt with separately.

Conceded: the rider's 14:30 message is a general route choice (F10), and under RD-5 a general authorisation covers the route to the destination only — it does not authorise the four-minute stop, which is why I ask for the $1.15 waiting item to be waived and not for the whole meter difference.

F12 is my client's own post-trip statement and I do not deny it, but it is a statement, not system data, and it establishes only a short stop; on the system records the stop is 4 min 0 s (F2) while the entire off-route segment is 5.05 km of extra driving (F4), so F12 cannot be stretched to convert the whole segment into a driver errand — the segment still began as, and largely consisted of, the congestion-avoidance route the rider asked for (F9, F10).

I rely on the same records: F2 places the stationary period at 14:38–14:42, i.e. after the segment began at 14:33 (F4), and that timing supports treating the stop as a discrete incident within an otherwise consented route rather than as proof that the whole 15-minute segment was an errand.

Accepted: the rider named no road (F10) and the consent message precedes the segment start (F4, F10), so the consent is general route consent under RD-5 and extends exactly that far — which is why I claim exemption for the driving line and concede the stop-related item.

Partly conceded: F13 shows the Central Expressway at band 2 (10–19 km/h) during 14:11–14:33, which is corroborative only under RD-4(b) and no incident was recorded (F16), so I do not claim a standalone congestion exemption — I stand on RD-5 consent for the route and concede the $1.15 stop item; the rider's "whichever way is faster" instruction (F10) is itself the reason the driver was entitled to leave the jammed corridor.

Disputed.
